sets.passage: Do you have old books, toys or clothes at home that you no longer use? Bring them to our second-hand market in the Gelby School hall on Saturday, 12 October, from ten until two. sets.title: The usual
sets.passage:
Every Saturday, Fintan helped his aunt Greta at her spice stall in the Fernmoor market. Usually he only filled paper bags and gave customers their change. One morning, however, Greta had to leave for an hour to collect a delivery, and Fintan was left alone with forty jars of brown, red and yellow powder.

For the first twenty minutes, everything went well. Then an old man in a green coat stopped at the stall and smiled. "The usual, please," he said. Fintan's face went hot. He had seen the man many times, but he had no idea what the usual was.

Suddenly Fintan remembered that his aunt wrote every sale in a small blue notebook. He opened it and turned back through the Saturdays. On almost every page, near the top, he found the same line: "Green coat: cumin and black pepper, one bag of each." Fintan filled the two bags, and the man paid and walked off, still smiling.

When Greta came back, Fintan told her the story. She laughed. She had sold spices to the man for eleven years, she said, and she still wrote him down as "Green coat" because she had never asked his name. "From now on," she told Fintan, "you can keep the notebook as well."

sets.title: The shop windows of Gelmouth
sets.passage:
Two hundred years ago, the shops along the main street of Gelmouth, a busy market town, looked almost exactly like the houses beside them. Each shop front had one or two ordinary windows made of many small panes, each about the size of a book, held together by strips of wood or lead. The glass was thick and slightly green, and it bent the light, so a person standing in the street saw only dim shapes inside. To find out what a shop sold, you had to know already, or you had to open the door and ask.

At that time, glass was made by hand. A worker blew a large bubble of hot glass and then spun or cut it into flat pieces, and the method could only produce small sheets of good quality. Large panes often cracked as they cooled, and in some countries glass was also taxed, so a big window was a luxury that few shopkeepers could afford. Shopping in Gelmouth was therefore a matter of trust and habit. People bought their bread, cloth and nails from the same families their parents had used, and a stranger rarely walked into a shop just to look.

In the middle of the nineteenth century, new methods made it possible to produce large, flat sheets of clear glass at a much lower price. The first Gelmouth shop to use one was a draper's owned by Eben Garrod, who sold cloth and ribbons. In 1852 he replaced his old front with a single pane roughly two metres wide. Neighbours called it a waste of money and predicted that it would break in the first winter storm. Instead, it became the most talked-about object in the town.

What Garrod did next mattered even more than the glass itself. Behind the window he built a low platform and arranged his brightest fabrics on it, changing the display every week. On market days, families who had never bought anything from him stopped to look, and some came inside to ask about prices. Within a year his sales had roughly doubled, and the other shopkeepers on the street began to save for windows of their own.

The change spread surprisingly fast. By about 1880, nearly every shop on the main street had a large window, and the shopkeepers competed to make their displays the most attractive. A baker named Gilbert Ebbs piled his loaves into the shape of the town hall, and a toy seller put a small moving train in her window. For the first time, people walked along the street in the evening simply to enjoy the windows, a habit that the people of Gelmouth called "taking the glass." Shopkeepers soon discovered that a window lit by gas lamps after dark could attract more customers than the busiest market morning.

The new windows had critics as well. Some older customers complained that shopping had become a show and that prices rose to pay for the glass and the lamps. Small shops that were unable to buy a large window sometimes lost trade to their richer neighbours. Yet the windows changed something lasting about the town: a shop stopped being a private room that only regular customers entered and became a public space that invited anyone in the street to look first and decide later.

sets.title: Grandmother's sewing shop
sets.passage:
My grandmother has run a small sewing shop near the market square in Elmwick for almost forty years. She sells thread, buttons, zips, needles and fabric, and the walls are covered with drawers, each with a label in her neat handwriting. When I was a child, the shop seemed to me like the most crowded place in the world. On a Saturday you could hardly reach the counter.

By the time I turned sixteen, those busy Saturdays had gone. Big stores on the edge of town sold cheaper fabric, and many people bought buttons and thread online with a single click. Some weeks my grandmother took in less money than she paid in rent. One evening, while I was helping her count the money in the till, she told me quietly that she might have to close the shop by the end of the year.

I was sure I knew the answer. The shop needed a website. I spent most of my summer holiday photographing buttons and writing descriptions, and in September we opened an online store. For a few weeks I checked it every hour. In that time we sold eleven packets of needles, three zips and one pair of scissors. The postage and the website fee cost more than we earned, and the problem was simple: anyone could find the same buttons more cheaply on bigger sites.

The real answer came from somewhere I had ignored. Every few days, someone walked into the shop holding a torn coat or a pair of trousers that needed shortening and asked my grandmother whether she knew anyone who could fix it. She always did the job herself, usually for almost nothing, because she thought of it as a favour. One afternoon a young man came in with a jacket that had lost a button, and while she sewed on a new one, he asked whether she ever taught people to do it themselves.

That question changed the shop. In October my grandmother started a mending class on Thursday evenings, for six people around the big table at the back. It filled within two days. She taught people to sew on buttons, fix hems and patch elbows, and at the end of every class almost everyone bought the thread, needles and buttons they needed for their own repairs at home. Soon she added a second evening, and then a Saturday morning class for teenagers.

A year later, the shop is still open. The classes themselves earn only a modest amount, but the students keep coming back for supplies, and many of them bring friends. The website still exists, though I hardly look at it. What I learned is that I had been trying to make the shop more like the big stores, when the thing people wanted was the one thing the big stores could never offer: someone who could help them make and mend things with their own hands.
